title: What Does It Take to Find Success as a Bar in New York City Right Now? 5 Top Operators Weigh In.

content:
There’s no market like New York City. Across all industries, businesses operate in a distinct landscape that offers both boundless opportunities and challenges. The city is incredibly dense with cultural influence, diverse consumer demographics, and economic power, creating a fertile ground for businesses to flourish.

But with those innumerous possibilities comes many roadblocks. The five boroughs are rife with competition: An up-and-coming chef trying to convert their pop-up series into a brick and mortar must vie with the city’s most prestigious restaurant empires to have a chance at survival. Not to mention the tight streets, small storefronts, high rents, and ever-increasing costs of labor and ingredients. On top of it all, consumers’ penny pinching continues to threaten the stability of the city’s bars and restaurants. Beverage programs were once the lifeline of the hospitality industry, but consumers are now cutting back on how much they spend on booze while dining out, forcing operators to adjust.

Put simply, running a hospitality business in NYC can be a ruthless game. Sure, “if you can make it here, you can make it anywhere” — but actually “making it” can be nearly impossible to accomplish. New Yorkers are notorious for their discerning taste and highly selective dining habits. In a city teeming with options, diners might consider a space’s design and ambiance; the value of its product; and the precision of its point of view.

With endless considerations, which decisions do bar owners think help move the needle toward success? We asked five of the city’s most accomplished operators what it actually takes to run a successful bar right now. Here’s what they said.

Chase Sinzer

Owner, Claud, Penny, and Stars

What brings people in is a combination of the team, the beverage curation, and the room. For Stars, we spent a lot of time curating our tiny space. We wanted the bar to feel inviting, welcoming, and warm. We’re constantly working on the room as a team through various channels while discussing how to make that inviting environment happen.

Our beverage program was designed to appeal to both the most discerning guest and a casual visitor that has never heard of us before. The wine program is the opposite of stagnant. We are working on it day in and out to ensure it has diversity and breadth — and the team behind it is excited to share it and meet guests where they are at.

Our 88 bottles under $88 section has also been a big calling card for Stars. Highlighting affordability is something we rock at the bar. It’s allowed people to feel comfortable in our space and never doubt that we have their back from an economic point of view. That also allows us to offer diversified price points without appearing top-heavy.

Overall, “making it” is maybe all about realizing you haven’t made it. We never believe we are at a plateau or have reached a place of true comfort, though that doesn’t mean that we don’t recognize success or give positive feedback. The key to the most competitive market in the world, though, is being thankful for your success and feeling grateful while always pushing for more through relentless self-critique.

Annie Shi

Owner, Lei; partner, King, Jupiter, and Dean’s

Lei is a transportative experience for guests, and I think that’s what people are looking for if they’re going to spend money by going out. They want to feel like they are in someone else’s world and that it’s a complete, immersive experience. Both Lei and Dean’s do that in their own fashion. You feel that in the atmosphere. What’s in your glass — whether a cocktail, perfectly pulled Guinness, or a great glass of wine — obviously matters, but the experience is also in all the details, from the lighting and the music to the service. Going out is very expensive right now, so every facet of a space has to hit.

I have been working in wine for 10 years now, and the price for a bottle of great white Burgundy in 2016 versus 2026 has tripled. Costs are a really tough pill to swallow, and one of our core missions at Lei is to inspire more people to want to become wine drinkers and wine lovers. One very specific pillar of that mission is to convert people who had only ever ordered a glass to have the confidence and the comfort to order a bottle. That transition from glass to bottle is really, really crucial in the journey of what it means to love and understand wine, and that’s why we price our bottles so fairly.

Fostering a space where guests feel comfortable ordering bottles is not just more economical for them, but much more enjoyable. A bottle of wine transforms from the moment you pull the cork to your last sip, and you can experience that when sharing a bottle of wine in a way that you simply don’t get when having a glass. It’s the joy and convivial nature of drinking wine with friends that makes it totally different than having a glass of wine for yourself at home, and that’s something we’ve captured at Lei.

Something that we care a lot about as a wine team is what, exactly, is tasting great, agnostic of region, winemaker, or price. Our wine director Matt Turner is tasting upwards of 50 wines a day, sometimes five days a week. In an environment where the blue-chip regions become more expensive than ever because they’re more in demand than ever, it is our responsibility as wine professionals to think about what value means for our guests. And that comes from tasting, tasting, tasting. That’s how we find up-and-coming regions and producers who are making wine with integrity and with great farming practices that can be sold at reasonable prices. That makes guests think, “I want to come back. Wine is not too expensive nor intimidating for me, and I feel comfortable ordering that bottle on the list.”

The ultimate key to making it in NYC is obviously the quality of your offering. New Yorkers are incredibly discerning. Your selection has to be on point, and you have a real perspective and point of view. As people choose to drink quality over quantity, you must have a great offering in a unique space. The atmosphere, the people watching, the glassware — all of that has to feed into the experience.

Steve Schneider

Bar manager and head bartender, Sip & Guzzle

Luck, timing, experience, and imagination — with location and providing a high-quality product also being important — are the four keys to success in this city. But I take pride in putting hospitality first. I just want to operate a really cool, unique spot and everything else falls in line from there.

Our dedication to hospitality and service aside, the variety of options we provide to all types of drinkers — with the addition of really good, fun food — keeps people coming in.

Environmentally, minimizing waste should be considered standard practice. Economically, the more you can use from one single item, the less expensive that item becomes. For instance, we use super high quality A5 Wagyu in our Royale With Cheese with the trimmings getting ground up to make our Tavern Burger and the fat rendered down to make our Wagyu Old Fashioned. The multiuse of such a high-quality ingredient is essential. Otherwise, it’s hard to use these ingredients at all because of the high price point per ounce.

Piper Kristensen

Beverage director, Redwood Hospitality (Place des Fêtes, Cafe Mado, and Golden Ratio)

The question of success is a tricky one. What are we measuring? Are my employees making enough money? Are we contributing to the community? Are we staying true to our concept and vision? Are we maintaining our values? Are we giving customers what they want? Am I making money? Is everyone, generally, having fun?

These are all markers of success in some way. Many are linked, and some are in direct opposition to one another. You will never get them all at once, and the balance can shift over time.

In my experience, the greatest driver to success is flexibility — specifically, the flexibility to change what you consider success to look like as the business evolves. Across Redwood Hospitality, our projects are all at different stages. Place des Fêtes and Cafe Mado are longer tenured and relatively well established, while Golden Ratio is still in its first year. Each location has different needs, so we can’t measure or manage them in the same ways.

Seasonality is one way that flexibility takes shape across our venues. It is a core value for us and gives us a regular reason to assess our systems. It keeps our food and beverage programs fresh and forces us to keep making edits to what should stay and what should go.

I don’t believe there is one formula for making it in New York. For us it means staying responsive to nature, to the business, to our teams, to the community, and to the customers.

Takuma Watanabe

Owner, Martiny’s, L’Americana, and Midnight Blue

One of the factors that consistently drives customers to Martiny’s is that our cocktail menu is constantly evolving. I don’t like creating cocktails under the pressure of a fixed schedule and am fortunate enough to travel around the world. I try to bring the inspiration I gain from those experiences back to the bar, making small updates to our menu every month.

Another reason might be something very simple: we genuinely enjoy making cocktails, and we take great pride in what we do. I believe our guests can feel that passion.

One of the most important elements to building a successful bar is to attend as many industry events and seminars as possible, so you can build relationships with others in the field and continue to grow within the community. I try to bring as many of my team members as I can to these events because I want them to meet new people and broaden their perspectives. Investing in opportunities for the team to engage with the industry is just as important as investing in their technical skills. The more experience they gain, the more they learn and grow — and they can then bring what they’ve acquired back to our own bar.

At the bar, we meet so many customers every single day. I think the real challenge is how well we can connect with our guests through both our hospitality and the product we offer. At the end of the day, it comes down to a simple question: Can we create an experience that genuinely resonates with people and makes them want to come back? That’s one of the simplest things to understand, but also one of the hardest qualities to consistently achieve.

*Quotes edited for clarity.

title: We Asked 10 Brewers: What’s the Most Underrated Cheap Beer? (2026)
summary:
When looking for quality brews, the word “cheap” can carry a negative connotation that makes some consumers shirk away. But there’s a wide world of crushable, delicious beers to be found on the lower end of the category’s price range. Craft beer purists may be surprised to learn that those who work in the industry, especially brewers, are often reaching for a budget brew that they swear by. So we went ahead and asked 10 brewers which so-called “cheap” beers deserve a little more notice and applause.

content:
When looking for quality brews, the word “cheap” can carry a negative connotation that makes some consumers shirk away. But there’s a wide world of crushable, delicious beers to be found on the lower end of the category’s price range.

Craft beer purists may be surprised to learn that those who work in the industry, especially brewers, are often reaching for a budget brew that they swear by. So we went ahead and asked 10 brewers which so-called “cheap” beers deserve a little more notice and applause. Some called out industry favorites while others delved into their memories for a nostalgic brew they associate with a loved one. And one brewer found a cheap beer to fall in love with on a blind date that was otherwise forgettable.

These brewers will tell you that a great beer can be found at any price point — and it may be sitting on the shelf at your local grocery store. There’s a reason certain mass-produced beers persist on the market. As the legendary lover of all things food and drink, Anthony Bourdain once said: “Good is indeed good forever.”

The most underrated cheap beers according to brewers are:

  • Narragansett
  • Coors Banquet
  • Henry Weinhard’s Private Reserve
  • Miller Genuine Draft
  • Tecate
  • Dale’s Pale Ale
  • Hamm’s
  • Montucky Cold Snacks
  • Pacifico

“My answer would have to be Narragansett. Without a doubt. I went on a blind date a few years back and had it on draft at a local bar. It was the only part of the date I remembered. I totally fell in love with it right then and there.” —Savannah Roberts, head brewer, Triple Crossing Brewing, Fulton, Va.

“I’ll say Coors Banquet even though I feel like that’s not even remotely a hot take amongst brewers. I’ve never been with a gathering of craft brewers west of the Mississippi that didn’t end up with everyone drinking Banquets.” —Mike Beebe, head brewer, Melvin Brewing Company, Alpine, Wyo.

“My answer would be Coors Banquet. I like that it’s very easy to drink, has a present malty sweetness, and has more body than other ‘cheap’ beers.” —Heather Opheim, brewer and bartender, Deviant Wolfe Brewing, Sanford, Fla.

“For the most underrated cheap beer, I’m gonna have to go with Henry Weinhard’s Private Reserve. Henry Weinhard was definitely one of my dad’s go-to beers. And having basically grown up with it, when I came of drinking age, I was seeking out other beers that weren’t my dad’s. So I went through a really long stretch of not drinking it. But a couple of years ago I was helping someone move, and they had Private Reserve. And I’ll be damned if that beer wasn’t refreshing as hell. Had a moment where I thought, ‘Sh*t, the old man knows his stuff!’” —Michael Daly, head brewer, Here Today Brewery and Kitchen, Seattle

“Sure everyone loves Miller High Life, and I myself have proclaimed many a time that ‘I like my Miller’s Lite and my Coors’ Heavy,’ but when it comes to underrated cheap beers, I’ve always hung my hat on a hook underneath a bar that is serving ice-cold Miller Genuine Draft. I’ll never forget those gold-and-black cans in my grandpa’s fridge, there’s still something joyously liberating in a pint of MGD… especially if you can actually find it on draught!” —Joseph Isaac, head brewer, Third Window Brewing Company, Santa Barbara, Calif.

“I think that the most underrated cheap beer in the market is Tecate. As a Latina, I might be biased. But I find Tecate crisp, crushable, and just perfect with a lime. The other day I went to a concert venue and had three 16 ounce Tecates. My bill was $10.40. I thought that was crazy — at a concert venue? I live in an affordable city, sure, but that tab was so cheap that the beer tasted even better. I don’t know if that makes any sense. But I enjoyed the hell out of it!” —Maria Shirts, brewer, Sapporo USA, Richmond, Va.

“An underrated cheap beer, in my opinion, has to be Dale’s Pale Ale. An old-school American Pale Ale for just $6 at my go-to beer bar in Brooklyn? Hard to beat that. Classic hop character, a balanced malt backbone, and that crisp, bitter finish that makes you want another sip.” —Bert Chery, brewer, Finback Brewery; owner and head brewer, Adapt Beer Project, Queens

“It’s only been the last couple of years that I learned about Hamm’s. I wish I had more access to it out in western Mass. because it would certainly be my go-to. The 12 ounce, easy drinking can is a gem.” —Sarah Real, owner and head brewer, Hot Plate Brewing Co., Pittsfield, Mass.

“I’m thinking Montucky. It’s always been a solid crushable light lager. At H-E-B grocery here, you can get a 30-rack for $25, and they still donate to local organizations in the communities where their beer is sold.” —Sarah Cervera, brewer, Big Country Organic Brewing, Austin

“I’m gonna go with Pacifico. It’s the perfect beer for a hot day in the backyard, and its price point is typically better than the other Mexican lagers you find in the grocery store. I find it to have a little less heft to it than a Modelo, but a little more character than a Corona, which, to me, is the balance that I’m looking for in a cheap beer that you can drink all day” —Bobby Sciacca, brewer, King’s County Brewer’s Collective, Brooklyn

title: Anheuser-Busch CEO Brendan Whitworth Leaving to Lead Luxury Gym Chain Equinox
summary:
On Monday, Anheuser-Busch announced chief executive officer Brendan Whitworth will leave his post at the end of the month after five years in the role. He is departing the company to take on the position of CEO at luxury gym chain Equinox. Whitworth joined Anheuser-Busch in 2013 and was named CEO in July 2021. According to the release, his successor will be announced in “due course,” and Michel Doukeris, the current CEO of AB InBev will take over Whitworth’s responsibilities in the interim.

The article Anheuser-Busch CEO Brendan Whitworth Leaving to Lead Luxury Gym Chain Equinox appeared first on VinePair.
content:
On Monday, Anheuser-Busch announced chief executive officer Brendan Whitworth will leave his post at the end of the month after five years in the role. He is departing the company to take on the position of CEO at luxury gym chain Equinox.

Whitworth joined Anheuser-Busch in 2013 and was named CEO in July 2021. According to the release, his successor will be announced in “due course,” and Michel Doukeris, the current CEO of AB InBev will take over Whitworth’s responsibilities in the interim.

Whitworth’s tenure will likely be most remembered by the controversy surrounding a March Madness campaign for But Light with transgender influencer Dylan Mulvaney. The social media partnership, first posted in April 2023, incited a boycott of Bud Light that resulted in a major ding in sales. And Whitworth’s wishwashy response to the situation stirred up even more backlash for the brand. In the fallout, Bud Light lost its reigning spot as the most popular beer in the country, first giving up the crown to Modelo in 2023 and now trailing the new best-selling beer, Michelob Ultra, as of 2025.

In a major pivot from beer, Whitworth will now sink his teeth into the wellness and exercise industry. Equinox is a subscription-based, premium fitness club with locations in the U.S., Canada, and U.K.

title: Where To Drink in NYC Right Now (November 2026)
summary:
When the VinePair team isn’t busy working at HQ, we’re in the field doing what we do best: scoping out the best cocktails, wine, and beer in the five boroughs. Here are the cool, current, and flat-out excellent bars and restaurants you should visit in New York right now, according to our editors. Check here each month for an updated list of where to drink in New York City. New to the list this month: Bar à Part, Saint Denis, June Baby, Iara, and Crybaby.

content:
When the VinePair team isn’t busy working at HQ, we’re in the field doing what we do best: scoping out the best cocktails, wine, and beer in the five boroughs. Here are the cool, current, and flat-out excellent bars and restaurants you should visit in New York right now, according to our editors.

Check here each month for an updated list of where to drink in New York City. New to the list this month: Bar à Part, Saint Denis, June Baby, Iara, and Crybaby.

Bar Chimera

550 Madison Ave, New York, NY 10022

Part of Gracious Hospitality’s massive Midtown expansion — including a new location of Cote and a forthcoming omakase restaurant — Bar Chimera brings together three distinct drinking concepts: Martinis, whiskey, and wine. The luxurious space focuses on splurge-worthy drinks including an extensive program of aged Madeiras, special pours of hard-to-find wines and spirits, and classic Martinis made with meticulously thought-out ingredients, even down to the water used to dilute the drink.

Website

Bar CC

85 10th Ave, New York, NY 10011

The team behind Chelsea’s swanky Crane Club is expanding with an equally luxe cocktail bar — complete with floor-to-ceiling drapery, velvet fabric walls, and hand-blown Venetian sconces. For this project, chef Melissa Rodriguez and restaurateur Jeff Katz tapped acclaimed bartender Harrison Ginsberg (previously of Overstory) to design the cocktail program. Bar CC’s menu features elegant takes on classics like the CC Martini made with a savory olive, pepper, and mignonette brine, and the Toasted Almond Sour, with gin, toasted almond, lemon, and Italian meringue.

Website

Graciela

81 Greenwich Ave, New York, NY 10014

Graciela is an Argentine tavern and steakhouse from Pablo Rivero, the restaurateur behind Buenos Aires destination Don Julio. Though the showy live-fire cooking and big cuts of meat are center stage, the menu offers an impressive range of must-order starters like the cheesy brócoli dip with almonds and breadcrumbs and the perfectly dense chickpea tart with provolone and smoked paprika. The lengthy wine list offers an appealing set of global selections, but it’s hard to ignore the call to go all-in on the Argentina of it all. The program goes far beyond the obligatory Malbec, showcasing interesting bottles and producers not often seen on NYC lists. We recommend chatting with the wonderful team led by beverage director Jirka Jireh Rivera, to learn more about these lesser-known bottles the country has to offer, from high-elevation Sémillon to old-vine Bastardo.

Website

Bar à Part

72 Bedford St, New York, NY 10014

Bar à Part is a cozy new wine bar in the West Village from the team behind the beloved Provençal restaurant Zimmi’s (and conveniently located right next door). Bar à Part is the latest in a string of petite wine bars with heavy-hitting programs to open in NYC: The small 15-seat space offers a list of niche finds from across the south of France, northern Spain, and beyond. Though wine is the focus, you can still find a selection of small plates like ratatouille, crab tarts, and oeufs mayo written up on the chalkboard each day.

Website

Bar Etienne

44 Bedford St, New York, NY 10014

Another addition to downtown’s growing list of scene-y bars to sip a spritz and a tomato-adorned Martini, Bar Etienne recently opened in the former Bandits space in the West Village. The casual neighborhood spot from longtime friends and hospitality veterans Michael Bray and Keith Larry features a French bistro-inspired menu and a playful list of culinary-minded cocktails like the Banana Question, made with rum and clarified banana, and the Petite Pompette with strawberry infused Pimm’s and mint. And be sure to check out the menu of teeny ’tinis, including classic, dirty, mushroom, and tomato variations.

Website

Somssi

79 MacDougal St, New York, NY 10012

Somssi is a new restaurant from the team at NA:EUN Hospitality — the group behind acclaimed concepts Atoboy, Atomix, and NARO — spearheaded by the group’s former director of operations Ahris Kim. Between the diverse menu of shareable plates and the extensive selection of wine, sake, and cocktails, there are countless pairing permutations to be made here. One that calls to us is the Potato, Potato, Potato, and caviar, which neatly wraps a creamy pomme purée with thin, crispy potato strings, topped with a heap of caviar, of course, which we’re sure would go well with a sparkling wine from the Finger Lakes or even a spritzy sake. The menu is a treasure trove of interesting beverages, so whichever combo you go with, it’s bound to be a delightful drinking experience.

Website

Saint Denis

490 LaGuardia Pl, New York, NY 10012

While many new restaurants are pushing the boundaries of what a “bistro” can be, SoHo’s Saint Denis leans into the classic French bistro vibe. The buzzy, dimly lit space offers traditional dishes like a silky chicken liver mousse and a perfectly peppery petit filet au poivre alongside a great list of wines by-the-glass and a cocktail menu curated by beverage director Sarah Morrissey. For something out of the box, try the Fiorello Shandy, which supplements Guinness with peach whiskey and an orange slice, but to embrace that bistro feeling, get the Cold Shoulder Martini with vodka, fig leaf, and saline.

Website

Dean’s

213 6th Ave, New York, NY 10014

Just when we thought NYC’s Guinness mania couldn’t go any longer, Dean’s arrives in the West Village ready to pour you a perfect — and sometimes even oyster-topped — pint. The British pub-inspired spot from Jess Shadbolt and Annie Shi of King stays true to its theme with dishes like fish and chips, stargazy pie, and pork scratchings plus a list of English sparkling to wash it all down.

Website

Don’t Be Shy

68 Charlton St, New York, NY 10014

The latest in a string of cocktail bars inspired by Japanese craftsmanship and hospitality, Don’t Be Shy is a sleek new spot in Hudson Square inspired by the bars of Tokyo’s polished Ginza neighborhood. The signature “Trip to Japan” cocktails showcase Japanese flavors like the Edo, made with sweet potato miso flavored vodka, and the refreshing Echigo, which combines sparkling sake with Echigo stout beer.

Website

Noury

137 Sullivan St, New York, NY 10012

From Lina Goujjane and Alex Chang, the wife-and-husband team behind Hudson Square’s Kiko, Noury combines elements of a modern Japanese izakaya with those of a wine and sake bar. Here, guests can pair small bites like the daily selection of sashimi or the house vegetable futomaki with rare bottles of sake or splurge-worthy Champagnes.

Website

June Baby

197 2nd Ave, New York, NY 10003

East Village newcomer June Baby is a lively Filipino-American neighborhood bar from industry vets Roxanne Diaz Bangalan, Darwin Pornel, and Ben Rojo. The cocktail menu aims to bring nostalgic flavors to New York via ingredients and traditions from the team’s Filipino-American upbringings with drinks like the Turon-Tado — a caramelized banana and jackfruit Daiquiri riff — and the Calamansi Hi-Ball, and bites like the salt and pepper kanto fried chicken wings.

Website

Bar Monto

61 2nd Ave, New York, NY 10003

If you’ve been keeping up with New York’s boom in modern Irish pubs, here’s another one to add to your list. Bar Monto is the latest laid-back spot slinging creamy pints of Guinness in custom glassware. Beyond beer, the bar also offers a fun list of straightforward yet complex cocktails like the Basque Connection, made with Boatyard Irish gin, sherry, Valentia Island Irish vermouth, tonic, and muddled orange. The space draws inspiration from the pubs and social clubs found in Ireland in the 1980s and ’90s and aims to be a center for community, collaborating with local artists and musicians for events.

Website

Iara

205 Allen St, New York, NY 10002

Iara is a new restaurant from Brazilian-American chef Vitor Mendes, previously of beloved Brooklyn haunt Theodora. The menu is designed to express the flavors of the Brazilian Amazon, with dishes like the Moqueca, a Brazilian red snapper stew with red palm dende oil, coconut milk, and tucupi; and the Picanha com Fritas, a sirloin grilled over charcoal with cassava fries, served with açaí ketchup. Behind the stick is fellow Theodora alum Calvin Czypinski, mixing up cachaça-centric cocktails and interesting riffs like a Martini infused with flavors of guava and cheese.

Website

Tin’s

109 Ludlow St, New York, NY 10002

Tin’s is a multi-concept space from Philip Dizard and Mercury Tin, bringing together their love for New York bars and Shanghainese comfort food in a three-story experience that includes both a casual dumpling counter and high-end cocktail bar. Creative concoctions span from unexpected delights like the Timmy’s Brain Blaster, a bright-green frozen Cognac cocktail topped with salted mascarpone foam, to riffs on classics like the Dako-Ri, a classic Daiquiri made with maojian tea and lemongrass.

Website

Crybaby

153 Bowery, New York, NY 10002

Crybaby is a wine and cocktail bar focusing on Alpine regions, with bottles from across areas like the Jura, Savoie, and Switzerland, and, of course, a hefty Chartreuse collection. If you’ve been searching for a place to dive into a list of hard-to-find Jura wines while nursing a freezer Martini in a plush pink velvet chair, this is your new spot.

Website

Echo Lake

357 Grand St, Brooklyn, NY 11211

This new two-story bar concept in Williamsburg is entirely focused on celebrating rum. The first floor, Echo Lake, showcases the versatile spirit in a range of cocktails, from classic spirit-forward creations to fruit-filled tropical drinks. It also offers a full menu of Daiquiri variations, including a rotating “Daily Daiquiri” for just $12. Head downstairs to Undercurrent to dive deeper into the spirit with special pours from rare and hard to find bottles.

Website

Kinda Nice

168 Borinquen Pl, Brooklyn, NY 11211

Known for their work behind the bar at Brooklyn’s beloved Grand Army, Patty Dennison and Ally Marrone are going out on their own with their new venture Kinda Nice. The welcoming Williamsburg cocktail bar brings the convivial feeling of an old-school neighborhood diner, with the food and drinks to match. The cocktails are based on classic diner favorites, including a Greek Salad ‘Tini and a Short Stack Margarita (with a choice between strawberry and blueberry flavors).

Website

Titán

5 Front St, Brooklyn, NY 11201

With chef Alan Delgado of flour-tortilla destination Los Burritos Juarez designing the menu and esteemed bartender Ivy Mix, previously of beloved agave bar Leyenda and current co-owner of Whoopsie Daisy, shaking up drinks, Dumbo’s new Titán brings two buzzy names from New York’s food and drink scenes into one beautifully curated space. The drinks menu offers expertly executed classics like a Margarita and Michelada, as well as culinary-inspired cocktails like the Dirty Root, with bacanora and escabeche, and the frozen Charmagoy, which brings together tequila, tamarind, mango, and chamoy.

Website

Frenzie

129 Atlantic Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11201

 

The team behind Brooklyn’s Confidant is expanding with a casual pizza spot that caters to the late-night crowd. While Frenzie is sure to be a great place to enjoy a bottle of chilled red wine and a spicy vodka pie at any time, it’s worth noting that at 10 p.m. the restaurant offers a few combo deals that make for the perfect nightcap (every night out should end with a slice). The offer, available Thursday, Friday, and Saturday, pairs a cheese or pepperoni pie with either a pitcher of Narragansett beer, two Daiquiris, or two Martinis.

Website

Grimm Tavern

659 Vanderbilt Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11238

Lauren and Joe Gimm, the couple behind East Williamsburg’s beloved brewery Grimm Artisanal Ales, recently debuted their new restaurant Grimm Tavern. Here guests can explore Grimm’s extensive list of beers alongside classic American tavern dishes like a dry-aged smash burger and a muffuletta. But it isn’t just for beer fans; the menu also features a selection of wines from Grimm’s project Physica Wines as well as a list of signature cocktails.

Website

Zig Zag Oyster Bar

406 Prospect Pl, Brooklyn, NY 11238

The team behind Lower East Side seafood hot spot Cervo’s now has a dedicated raw bar in Brooklyn. If indulging in a seafood tower could ever be considered casual, this vibey, walk-in only spot might be the place. Grab a seat on the sidewalk or along the space’s stunning curved bar and order an Original Martini or Bloody Mary to accompany the icy plates of oysters and shrimp cocktail.

Website

Bar Ferdinando

151 Union St, Brooklyn, NY 11231

Bar Ferdinando is an Italian bar and café that recently took over the space of beloved Carroll Gardens institution Ferdinando’s Focacceria, which served the neighborhood for 121 years. The revamped space pairs Sicilian snacks with classic aperitivo drinks and a wide selection of amari. It’s the ideal location for an afternoon of sipping Negronis, vermouth on the rocks, or even a strawberry-and-basil-infused Campari and Soda. And the refreshing drinks are the perfect pair for dishes like the pane e panelle, a sandwich stacked with crispy chickpea fritters, ricotta, and caciocavallo cheese, or the heaping plate of fries topped with garlicky clams.

Website

Tavern Next Door

327 Van Brunt St, Brooklyn, NY 11231

If you’ve ever found yourself waiting for over two hours to snag a bite of Red Hook Tavern’s thick, pepper-crusted burger, we have the cocktail bar for you. The meat-slinging team recently expanded with a next-door cocktail bar that not only features one of the city’s most coveted burgers, but a whimsical cocktail menu with brightly colored creations like the tall, neon Blue Hawaiian and a refined take on an Appletini.

Website

Mash Inn

1215 8th Ave, Brooklyn, NY 11215

Located in a former laundromat in Park Slope, Mash Inn is a new bar and beer counter from the team behind Gold Star in Prospect Heights. The casual spot offers a rotating menu of beers on draft that you can enjoy in the cozy record-filled space or order growlers to-go from the beer window. The bar also offers light snacks like cheese, pickles, and charcuterie to enjoy alongside the freshly poured pints.

title: The Best Bottle of Whiskey for Each Classic Cocktail, According to Bartenders
summary:
Whiskey has always played a key role in the world of mixed drinks. The Old Fashioned is widely considered to be the world’s first cocktail, a foundation that eventually spun off into a wide range of classics like the Manhattan, Sazerac, and the Whiskey Sour. Though it’s easy to marry the robust, sugary, and sometimes spicy flavor profile of the brown spirit with other liquors and ingredients, choosing the right bottle is key to maximizing each cocktail. Deciding between bourbon and rye for a whiskey-based cocktail is one thing; picking exactly which brand and expression is an entirely different ballgame.

The article The Best Bottle of Whiskey for Each Classic Cocktail, According to Bartenders appeared first on VinePair.
content:
Whiskey has always played a key role in the world of mixed drinks. The Old Fashioned is widely considered to be the world’s first cocktail, a foundation that eventually spun off into a wide range of classics like the Manhattan, Sazerac, and the Whiskey Sour. Though it’s easy to marry the robust, sugary, and sometimes spicy flavor profile of the brown spirit with other liquors and ingredients, choosing the right bottle is key to maximizing each cocktail.

Deciding between bourbon and rye for a whiskey-based cocktail is one thing; picking exactly which brand and expression is an entirely different ballgame. The best whiskey for, say, a Boulevardier is likely different from the best for a Paper Plane. Seasoned drinkers may prefer a high-proof expression that can stand up to other ingredients in complicated cocktails, whereas whiskey newcomers may like beginner-friendly bottles with mellow, welcoming flavors.

So, we tapped 10 bartenders from around the country to name the bottles of whiskey they reach for when building an Old Fashioned, Manhattan, Whiskey Sour, and a wild card cocktail of their choice. Their answers range in proof, style, and mash bill — all dependent on personal preference.

Brandon Judd

Beverage manager, Camel Club, Lexington, Ky.

Old Fashioned: I’ve always preferred rye in an Old-Fashioned, partly out of respect for the cocktail’s history, but Old Bardstown Bottled-in-Bond makes a compelling case for bourbon. Its 100-proof structure stands up beautifully to rich demerara syrup and aromatic bitters, while a touch of orange bitters and an expressed lemon twist bring the whole drink into focus.

Manhattan: I prefer rye in a Manhattan because its spice creates a necessary counterpoint to the richness of sweet vermouth. Rittenhouse Bottled-in-Bond Rye delivers enough weight and character at 100 proof to maintain that tension while allowing the vermouth and bitters to contribute their own complexity.

Whiskey Sour: Elijah Craig Small Batch has the balance of fruit, oak, and warm spice that I want in a Whiskey Sour. At 94 proof, it maintains a noticeable whiskey presence against the acidity of fresh lemon while its natural sweetness helps bring the cocktail together.

Boulevardier: I like my Boulevardiers whiskey-forward, typically using one and a half ounces of rye, although I wouldn’t argue with someone pouring two. Old Forester 100 Proof Rye has the spice, citrus, and backbone to stand up to Campari and sweet vermouth, creating a cocktail where the whiskey leads without sacrificing the beautiful bitterness that makes a Boulevardier so compelling.

Toby Maloney

Co-author, The Classic Cocktail Sessions; owner, The Elbow Room, Vancouver, Wash.

Old Fashioned: Old Forester Signature 100 Bourbon. I like to use a 100-proof whiskey in my Old Fashioned because I want the narrative arc to last for a slow sipper, starting a bit sweet and hot for the first few sips before settling into all its glory as the big ice cube melts. The last sip should still have a defined whiskey presence, so a big personality is key.

Manhattan: Rittenhouse Rye Bottled-in-Bond. As a Manhattan warms, it gets more nuanced and boozy. I love those last couple of sips when it’s sidling up to room temperature. The key is a spicy rye whiskey that can stand up to a big vermouth, such as Carpano Antica Formula, because the marriage of spirit and aromatized wine makes this cocktail pure bliss.

Whiskey Sour: Wild Turkey 101 Rye. I like my whiskies in triple digits, and this delightful distillate, idiomatically referred to as the Kickin’ Chicken, is great in egg white drinks that need a longer shake for proper aeration than regular sours.

Ward Eight: Copper & Kings Straight Bourbon Whiskey finished in American apple brandy barrels. This whiskey adds an unexpected orchard note to the cocktail and dries out its sweetness. Working with whiskeys that have utilized brandies first make for great complex cocktails.

Ricky Dolinsky

Beverage director, Dandelion and Keepers, New York City

Old Fashioned: Hillrock Solera Aged Bourbon is a beautiful whiskey from upstate New York that was aged via the solera method, adding a sweet nuttiness. Expressing an authentic sense of terroir from the region, use it to build a New York Old Fashioned with locally made sorghum syrup and black walnut bitters.

Manhattan: Old Grand-Dad 114. Old Grand Dad Bottled-in-Bond has been my well whiskey for many years. There is hardly a better bang-for-buck, and it punches well above its weight in any whiskey cocktail. Because of its high rye mash bill, I find it sings best when paired with sweet vermouth, such as in a Manhattan or Boulevardier. The OGD 114 proof makes for a tantalizing concoction of a Manhattan: strong, viscous, and balances the perfect tension between boozy, sweet, and spicy.

Whiskey Sour: Yellowstone Bourbon 86. Of all the heritage brands, Yellowstone does the best of bridging tradition with modernity. The whiskey always tastes like it comes from a dusty bottle that had been long forgotten in your grandpa’s cabinet while still being able to translate compelling flavors through cocktails. In a Whiskey Sour, notes of pecan and brown sugar take me close to pecan pie notes without dominating the palate with sweetness. It’s truly a gift of a bourbon.

Paper Plane: Old Forester 86 Proof. My main complaint with Paper Planes is when a cheaper bourbon is used and all you can taste is oak and vanilla. Old Forester has enough esters to take away from that, leading to a cocktail that has more spice and fruit than oak. Those notes mingle harmoniously with amaro and Aperol, rounding out a drink that is the perfect blend of sweet, spiced, bitter, and refreshing.

Molly Horn

Chief mixologist and spirits educator, Total Wine & More, Washington, D.C.

Old Fashioned: I reach for a bourbon that has a good bite to it — a little overproof with a high rye mash bill, so both the heat and the spicy backbone stand up to this cocktail’s sweetness. Wolcott Rickhouse Reserve Bourbon is a great example of this style, coming in at 120 proof and packing a lot of bold, complex oak and peppery spice notes.

Manhattan: This is when things can get a little contentious: rye or bourbon? I’ll admit, my gateway Manhattan was actually a wheated bourbon version, but as I’ve developed my palate, my new favorite is a rich and full-bodied rye. Still Austin’s “The Artist” is an excellent everyday rye with a lot of spice and dark fruit notes that play well with sweet vermouth. If I want to treat myself, Angel’s Envy Rye finished in Caribbean Rum Casks layers in a rich, tropical fruit character that takes a classic Manhattan to the next level.

Whiskey Sour: A dive bar Whiskey Sour might make you think that there isn’t a lot of artistry behind this cocktail, but a good whiskey and proper technique can elevate this simple drink to a memorable experience. Because you’re adding sweetness (sugar), sourness (lemon), and texture (egg white) for the drink’s other components, I find that an intense, oaky bourbon is the key to achieving perfect balance, which is why I like to use Knob Creek bourbon. With its high proof point and deep, charred wood character, it really shines in this simple recipe.

Boulevardier: My husband’s favorite cocktail is a Boulevardier, and I find that the build is a really flexible blueprint that works with many different styles of bourbon. I recently started using Center Stave, and it brings delicious results. It’s an 88-proof port cask-finished bourbon that has rich and nutty stewed fruit notes on the finish along with caramel, vanilla, and a lingering spice character.

Hannah Hulsey

Head bartender, FKA: Formerly Known As, NYC

Old Fashioned: I always reach for Elijah Craig. It’s smooth and smoky with a subtle spice, beautifully rounded out by bitters and an expressed orange peel.

Manhattan: My ideal whiskey for Manhattan is Rittenhouse. Its strong constitution stands in delicious solidarity with vermouth.

Whiskey Sour: Four Roses is perfectly suited for whiskey sour. The subtle sweetness of the whiskey is a lovely balance for the punchiness of lemon juice, resulting in a smooth, delicious cocktail.

Sazerac: A Sazerac is an unbeatable cocktail, especially if made with Michter’s Rye. The notes of oak, pepper, and butterscotch give the green fairy a lovely place to land.

Jennifer Yim

Master mixologist, Bellagio Resort & Casino, Las Vegas

Old Fashioned: I’d go with Four Roses Small Batch. It has a lovely balance of ripe fruit, caramel, and warm baking spices, with a soft, rounded mouthfeel. I love how a little sugar, bitters, and proper dilution open up those flavors while letting the bourbon speak for itself.

Manhattan: I’d recommend Still Austin Single Barrel Rye. I love the richness and depth it brings, with layers of oak, peppery spice, and a lingering warmth. That spice cuts through the sweetness of the vermouth, giving the cocktail a beautiful balance and a nice, structured finish.

Whiskey Sour: Wild Turkey 101 is my pick. I love its full-bodied richness, with notes of caramel, vanilla, and toasted oak. The higher proof brings more intensity and complexity, allowing the bourbon’s character to shine through the fresh citrus while maintaining a beautiful balance of sweetness and acidity.

Vieux Carré: One of my favorite whiskey cocktails is the Vieux Carré. I love how it brings together the richness of Cognac, the spice of rye, and the herbal complexity of sweet vermouth and Bénédictine. I enjoy using High West Rendezvous Rye because its warm spices, subtle herbal notes, and rich texture add beautiful depth while keeping all those layers in harmony.

Ektoras Binikos

Co-founder, Atheras Spirits, Bitter Monk, and Sugar Monk, NYC and Brooklyn

Old Fashioned: I highly recommend Four Roses Single Barrel Bourbon. Its luxurious chocolate notes, complemented by hints of oak and a delightful nutty texture, create a beautifully balanced drink.

Manhattan: Michter’s US*1 Single Barrel Straight Rye is my pick. This whiskey offers exquisite flavors of butterscotch, white pepper, juicy melon, and a hint of baking spice, making it the perfect companion to a rich Italian vermouth with a strong wormwood presence.

Whiskey Sour: Elijah Craig Small Batch Bourbon is the way to go. With a proof of 94, it boasts a robust character that imparts deep flavors of toasted oak, baking spice, and honey, enhancing the cocktail magnificently.

Paper Plane: I choose Wild Turkey 101 Bourbon. Its high proof ensures it stands up brilliantly to the citrus and harmonizes seamlessly with the amaro and Aperol, allowing all the intricate flavors to emerge for a truly complex experience.

Lauren Pizzo

Head bartender, Streetlight Taco, Tampa, Fla.

Old Fashioned: An Old Fashioned should showcase the whiskey, with sugar and bitters simply enhancing what’s already there. Elijah Craig Small Batch delivers with its 94-proof backbone, rich vanilla, toasted oak, and deep Kentucky bourbon heritage. It has the structure and complexity to shine without needing much help.

Manhattan: A great Manhattan deserves a rye with character, and Michter’s rye brings plenty of it. Its warming baking spices, subtle citrus, and peppery finish beautifully complement the caramel sweetness and herbaceous complexity of sweet vermouth, creating a rich and balanced cocktail.

Whiskey Sour: A Whiskey Sour needs a bourbon bold enough to stand up to lemon, sugar, and egg white. Old Grand-Dad 114 Single Barrel 7-Year Bourbon high-rye mash bill and high proof delivers plenty of spice, oak, and richness, giving the cocktail a strong backbone without overpowering its refreshing balance.

Brown Derby: Basil Hayden Toast uses brown rice instead of rye in its mash bill. That removes the peppery spice that can sharpen against grapefruit’s bitterness and the rice gives a softer, slightly nutty, cereal-sweet profile that lets the grapefruit taste bright rather than harsh. Its secondary finish in toasted (not charred) barrels leans toward caramelized sugar, toasted bread, and marshmallow rather than heavy char, and it plays nicely with honey as a compliment.

Tyler Davidson

Head Bartender, Monkey Thief, NYC

Old Fashioned: The first whiskey I think about when making an Old Fashioned is Rittenhouse. An Old Fashioned, for me, is meant to be a low-frills drink that really showcases the nature of whatever bottle you’re grabbing, so a nice bonded rye is a great start. Rittenhouse packs that necessary punch to start, and then backs it up with round flavors of baking spice and orange peel on the finish.

Manhattan: I usually gravitate more toward a rye that’s not too harsh around the edges. Michter’s Rye is a go-to for me: I find that the elegantly subtle bite combined with the sweet corn finish makes for a smooth sip and pairs nicely with many different styles of sweet vermouth.

Whiskey Sour: I typically will grab something a tad overproof to cut through the richness of the lemon, sugar, and egg white. Old Grand-Dad 114 is a bottle I’m always excited to mix with for a classic sour: Notes of vanilla come through to complement the bright flavors, yet it’s bold and spiced enough to ground the drink and linger on the palate.

Saratoga: One of my favorite classic cocktails that I don’t see around very often is a Saratoga, an equal-part split of rye, cognac, and sweet vermouth with a couple dashes of Angostura bitters. For this, I would go for something with some bold and rounded character to stand up well with the cognac, something like Jack Daniel’s Single Barrel Rye with its complex fruitiness.

Darryl Chan

Bar director, NoHo Hospitality Group, NYC

Old Fashioned: Knob Creek 9 Year Single Barrel Reserve Bourbon. Maybe it’s the change in weather, but I’m loving a good high-proof bourbon like this one: It won’t go flabby as it dilutes, and it has great notes of toasted nuts and charred oak. The bitters, rich syrup, and orange amplify all the goodness in this bottle.

Manhattan: Rittenhouse Rye. This is a nostalgic choice for me, since a certain Manhattan that a friend once made with Rittenhouse, Carpano Antica, and a healthy dash of Angostura opened my eyes to what the drink could be. Beyond the pepperiness, the rye’s dried fruit and toffee notes really sing with the vermouth, and the high proof reminds you to slow down and savor it.

Whiskey Sour: Booker’s — because why not? The high proof and sturdy tannins balance out the sweet and sour and make you appreciate the frothiness from the egg white.

Old Pal: Wild Turkey 101 Rye. My boss is a big fan of this drink, and so am I, especially since I love giving high-proof bottles a good home in a cocktail. This rye’s bright, high-toned flavors complement the Campari and dry vermouth in the best way.

title: Booze News Weekly Roundup: Judge Approves RNDC Chapter 11, Class Suit Brews Against Celsius, and More
summary:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Heineken’s memo about effects of weight-loss drugs on drinking, RNDC’s Chapter 11 liquidation, and a ton of product releases. News to know: Heineken alarms U.K. pubs of GLP-1 effects on booze purchases: Heineken warned of weight-loss drugs’ negative effects on alcohol purchases and suggested strategies for working around them in a document sent to U.K. bars and pubs.

The article Booze News Weekly Roundup: Judge Approves RNDC Chapter 11, Class Suit Brews Against Celsius, and More appeared first on VinePair.
content:
This is VinePair’s Booze News Weekly Roundup, where we gather the hottest headlines and product releases every Friday for a snapshot of what’s happening in the beverage alcohol industry. This week, we have updates on Heineken’s memo about effects of weight-loss drugs on drinking, RNDC’s Chapter 11 liquidation, and a ton of product releases.

News to know:

  • Heineken alarms U.K. pubs of GLP-1 effects on booze purchases: Heineken warned of weight-loss drugs’ negative effects on alcohol purchases and suggested strategies for working around them in a document sent to U.K. bars and pubs. The document, unsealed and reviewed by Reuters, marks one of the few times a major alcohol company has addressed potential setbacks to business caused by GLP-1s — earlier this year, executives at Diageo and Carlsberg both played down the suspicion that the drugs significantly curb alcohol consumption. Heineken, the second largest brewer in the world, urged pub and bar operators to serve half-pints, low- and non-alcoholic drinks, and smaller food plates.
  • Judge OKs RNDC’s Chapter 11 plan after settlement with unsecured creditors: A Texas judge approved Republic National Distributing Company’s (RNDC) Chapter 11 liquidation plan on Tuesday after the company reached a settlement with its unsecured creditors last week. RNDC, once the second-largest alcohol distributor in the U.S. before shedding nearly all of its business this past year, filed for bankruptcy in July.
  • Court denies Fawn Weaver’s motion to block Uncle Nearest sale: A U.S. court rejected Weaver’s motion to stop the sale of her embattled whiskey brand. Weaver filed the request for injunction earlier this month after Uncle Nearest’s court-appointed receiver Phillip G. Young, Jr., noted three potential buyers were actively eyeing the brand in a separate court filing.
  • Class suit brewing against Celsius’ “burns body fat” claims: A Washington State resident sued Celsius over “healthwashing” for making unsubstantiated claims that the energy drink “burns body fat.” The plaintiff Annabelle Nielsen is hoping to loop in other consumers to launch a class action lawsuit.

Product releases to watch:

  • Popular Prosecco brand adds first sparkling non-alcoholic wine to portfolio: La Marca, the top-selling Prosecco brand in the U.S., released its first-ever zero-proof sparkling wine. Made with carbonated de-alcoholized wine, the NA version of the beloved crisp, fruity bubbly is available nationwide for a suggested retail price of $18.99 per bottle.
  • 1792 releases a wheated, full-proof bourbon: The Bardstown, Ky.-based brand rolled out a wheated bourbon bottled at 125 proof. 1792 Wheated Full Proof Bourbon will be available next month in California, Florida, Illinois, Texas, and New York, for a suggested retail price of $39.99 per 375-milliliter bottle.
  • Four Roses debuted third Experimental Series bourbon: Four Roses’ latest addition to its Experimental Series is a bourbon finished in Japanese chestnut wood. Experimental Series No. 003: Chestnut is bottled at 104 proof and will be available at the Lawrenceburg and Cox’s Creek, Ky., visitor centers beginning Nov. 20 for a suggested retail price of $55 per 375-milliliter bottle.
  • The Whistler’s ‘Triple Oak’ blends three different whiskeys aged in three different casks: The Irish Whiskey brand’s newest release combines single pot still, single malt, and single grain whiskeys aged in ex-bourbon, Oloroso sherry, and PX sherry casks, respectively. The Whistler Triple Oak is now available nationwide for a suggested retail price of $29.99.
  • Blade and Bow bottles 30-year-old bourbon at cask strength: Blade and Bow unveiled a cask-strength expression of its esteemed 30-year bourbon. The limited release was distilled in 1993 and bottled three decades later at 164.2 proof. Just 30 bottles of the Blade and Bow 30-Year-Old Cask Strength will be available at the Stitzel-Weller Distillery beginning Oct. 30 for $2,500, followed by limited, drop-style releases to select markets.

title: After Going Mainstream, Has Pumpkin Beer Become a Regional Specialty Again?
summary:

content:
Earlier this month, Jack’s Abby Brewing in Framingham, Mass., cranked up the oom-pah tunes for Oktoberfest revelry featuring stein-hoisting contests, plump pretzels, and lots and lots of lager.

“We set our all-time sales record for the beer hall,” says Sam Hendler, CEO of parent company Hendler Family Brewing.

Unsurprisingly, golden Munich Fest and Copper Legend Oktoberfest lagers took the top draft sales slots. Third place welcomed an underdog: Pumpkin Crop, a spiced autumnal lager. “That’s different from 10 years ago when it was all German lagers at Oktoberfest,” Hendler says. Now people want to party with pumpkin beer. When it comes to drinkers losing their gourd, “Massachusetts is a pretty good bellwether for New England.”

Pumpkin beer’s popularity in New England dates to Colonial America when resourceful brewers embraced pumpkins as a cheap and plentiful fermentable. During craft beer’s late-20th century rise, the region’s breweries rebooted pumpkin ale as a spiced fall seasonal that tasted like boozy pumpkin pie.

“You can almost call it the original pastry beer,” says Phil Markowski, the brewmaster at Two Roads Brewing in Stratford, Conn.

Pumpkin beer hit a rough patch in the mid-2010s when market saturation and summertime releases sparked a backlash. Many pumpkin beers disappeared, but the style held strong in New England, fall’s wonderland of pumpkin patches, apple orchards, and leaf-peeping.

“These iconic seasonal moments create appetite and excitement for beers that echo the flavors and feelings of fall,” says Jon London, the head of beer at Boston Beer Company, which makes cinnamon-spiced Sam Adams Jack-O pumpkin ale.

Instead of dying on the vine, pumpkin beer today thrives as a regional specialty with deep-rooted preferences for time-tested brands. Born in 1996, Shipyard Brewing’s Pumpkinhead Ale still shines from its Portland, Maine headquarters down the East Coast. Across the country, Seattle’s Elysian Brewing first brewed the spiced Night Owl Pumpkin Ale in 1997, and the brand returns every fall.

“We love traditions and are creatures of habit, aren’t we?” says Jeff Richards, the senior marketing director at Elysian. “Pumpkin beer is one part of how we share in the spirit of the season.”

Why New England Is Awash in Pumpkin Beers

No region loves pumpkin beers more than New England. Over the past five years, Google Trends data show a concentration of interest in New England, with a pronounced spike this year. “Fall seasonal beers are more popular in New England than other areas of the country,” a Total Wine rep reported via email.

Pumpkin beer is “built into the culture,” says Rob Day, the vice president of marketing for Barrel One Collective, which encompasses 15 mainly New England brands including Harpoon, Smuttynose, Wachusett, and Long Trail. “People look forward to these moments.”

Barrel One sells seven different pumpkin beers and ciders, many with regional affinity. New Hampshire enjoys Smuttynose Pumpkin Ale, New Yorkers order Five Boroughs Pumpkin Ale, and Massachusetts drinkers crush Wachusett Pumpkin Ale.

“In each state, there’s a different pumpkin product in our portfolio that’s outperforming,” Day says. Sales of UFO Pumpkin are up 18 percent in Rhode Island, while Harpoon Pumpkin Cider is up 9.3 percent in Connecticut and Clown Shoes Pumpkin Sombrero is up 28 percent in New Hampshire.

“Fall seasonal beers are more popular in New England than other areas of the country.”

Pumpkin beer drinkers aren’t monolithic. For Hendler Family’s Massachusetts brands, flavor and ABV preferences vary across customer bases. Night Shift’s potent and strongly flavored Pumpkin Piescraper appeals to a younger, more urban crowd, Hendler shares, while Wormtown’s mellower, lower-alcohol Fresh Patch hits the blue-collar, more suburban customer base.

“The pumpkin beer phenomenon works across all demographics in Massachusetts,” Hendler says.

In Massachusetts, this fall’s most popular pumpkin beer is Shipyard Pumpkinhead, according to Circana data. “That’s our biggest market,” says Bruce Forsley, Shipyard’s president. Now 30 years old, Pumpkinhead accounts for almost half of Shipyard’s annual production and remains steady. “Craft beer has been struggling the last few years, but this segment remains healthy and robust with no immediate signs of decline,” Forsley says.

Shipyard is singularly focused on expanding and supporting the Pumpkinhead franchise. Smashed Pumpkin, the 9 percent ABV imperial pumpkin ale, continues to grow, and there’s also a version aged in bourbon barrels. This year, Shipyard also introduced an NA Pumpkinhead that sold out in three weeks. “We vastly underestimated the NA beer market,” says Forsley, who plans to boost production next year.

Pumpkin’s Fandom Spreads Wide

Thriving pockets of fandom expand beyond the Northeast, too, in part fueled by legacy brands. Southern Tier Brewing in Lakewood, N.Y., has ardent fans of Pumking Imperial Ale (born 2007) in New York State and adjoining regions; and Dogfish Head in Milton, Del., has legions of mid-Atlantic fans for Punkin Ale, first brewed in 1994.

Despite national interest seemingly waning, pumpkin beer sales are actually increasing in several surprising pockets. Shipyard ships Pumpkinhead Ale to 42 states. Georgia is growing, and “Florida is a very good market because New England transplants are down there,” Forsley says.

The challenge with wide distribution is a shorter selling season in warm-weather states. Pumpkin ale can be a tough sell when it tops 100 degrees in Texas, so distributors want to sell the beer in two or three weeks. “There’s not a traditional fall season,” he says. “There’s just the thought that, This is the time of year when I should have this beer.”

Heatwaves, though, aren’t a dealbreaker. Total Wine & More reports that searches for pumpkin products ramp up around the end of July, with a 210 percent increase from July 2020 to July 2026. And that warm-weather arrival of pumpkin beers is a feature, not a bug, of the complex beer-distribution system and demands of the calendar. “Seasonal creep” is just standard operating procedure for large brewers that need lead time for brewing, packaging, and shipping.

“Our distributors, by and large, will bring Pumpkinhead in July to be prepared to release it as soon as they have sold their last case of the previous seasonal beer, which is summer,” Forsley says. Could be mid-August, or maybe late July. “It’s based on depletion.”

“Craft beer has been struggling the last few years, but this segment remains healthy and robust with no immediate signs of decline.”

Boston Beer typically releases its fall seasonals, including Jack-O, during the first week of August. “That’s when people start craving fall,” London says. In a competitive sales landscape, “we want to be first to market with the seasonals people are excited about.”

Selling pumpkin beer earlier gives breweries a headstart on the style’s unofficial October 31 end date. “Even though pumpkin carries into Thanksgiving in such a big way, Halloween kind of ends pumpkin beer and you’re on your way out,” Day says.

Pumpkin Is an Invitation to Party

Encouraging customers to party maximizes the compressed sales season. This October, Two Roads hosted its eighth annual Roadsmary’s Baby Pumpkin Fest to celebrate its pumpkin beer partly aged in rum barrels. Attendees competed in pumpkin-carving competitions, watched The Ring, and ate pumpkin pie.

“The Northeast is known for pumpkin celebrations,” Markowski says, adding that Roadsmary’s Baby remains the top-selling Two Roads seasonal. Though volumes are down around 50 percent from the pre-pandemic peak, Two Roads still sells more than 1,000 barrels annually. “It’s here to stay,” he says.

Early October also marked Elysian’s 22nd annual Great Pumpkin Beer Festival. Nearly 3,000 people attended the block party to drink pumpkin ale poured from a hollowed-out 1,700-pound pumpkin. “We sold more beer on that Saturday night than we’ve ever sold on any single GPBF day,” Richards says. One-off releases keep interest high. Elysian has produced more than 100 different pumpkin beers over the years, including a pumpkin cheesecake ale and a pumpkin sour ale.

“The ability to create novelty around the familiar each year is so cool,” he says.

Beer styles were once rooted in place and taste: crisply elegant kölsch in Cologne, Germany; acidic lambic in Brussels, Belgium; bitter West Coast IPAs in California. Now every beer can be made everywhere, recipes and processes replicated around the globe. Reverting pumpkin beers to regional specialties, only sold for a few short yet festive months, can rekindle what once made craft beer so special. Here’s a beer, only available for the here and now.

Check out Maine’s fall foliage, hit a pumpkin patch, then pop by a neighborhood bar for a Pumpkinhead pint rimmed with sugar and cinnamon. Says Forsley, “It’s truly an American experience.”

content:
When it comes to measurements, most people — including Americans themselves — are eager to criticize the United States for its rejection of the metric system. Instead of embracing international units of measurement like liters, meters, and grams, the U.S. Customary System opts for units like gallons, inches, and pounds. But in one instance when the U.S. required a certain industry to make the pivot to metric, many citizens were not so pleased.

On Jan. 1, 1980, the federal government passed a law that mandated the American liquor industry adopt metric system norms, converting the volume measurements on all spirits bottles in the U.S. to liters. (A law required wine bottles to convert to metric units the previous year.) The U.S. made the switch in an effort to streamline trading booze across borders — a shift the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, and Firearms had pushed for years.

But the law didn’t just change the numbers displayed on the side of each bottle — in changing the units, the booze industry also started producing an entirely new set of bottle sizes. And when the law went into effect at the start of 1980, observant shoppers noticed their go-to bottle of liquor had shrunk.

The bottles that notoriously took the hit were the “fifths,” which were popular among consumers for their convenient size and easy-to-remember name. Equal to one-fifth of a gallon, “fifths” came out to around 757 milliliters. But under the new law, those were replaced with 750 milliliter bottles to match the metric system’s standards. The law also instated five additional bottle volumes: 50 milliliters, 200 milliliters, 500 milliliters, 1 liter, and 1 ¾ liters.

A 7 milliliter decrease might seem like a drop in the bucket, and it is: A jigger equates to roughly 44 milliliters, meaning each fifth lost just a fraction of a shot. So, it might come as a surprise that the slight change in bottle size caused quite the uproar among consumers.

People were so outraged that the news usurped other, more impactful laws that came with the new decade — including a $0.20 raise to the federal minimum wage. The fifth was such a cultural touchpoint at the time that the alcohol industry’s new system dominated the conversation. On Dec. 31, 1979, the Washington Post published the headline “Era of the Fifth to End With New Year” and the subheadline “Introducing Smaller Fifths, Higher Taxes.”

While the switch to metric became mandatory in 1980, liquor companies began pivoting to the measurement system as early as 1976 as part of a multi-year effort to ease in the industry’s new sizings. Beyond “fifths,” others within the previous system had easy calling cards as well — such as “quart,” “half gallon,” and “gallon” — and over the course of those four transitional years, consumers and tradespeople alike were stuck in a firestorm over what to call the new sizes.

As the old sizes phased out, many pitched new monikers for customers to use when they entered a liquor store. For instance, the Distilled Council Spirits Council of the United States (DICSUS) proposed referring to 200-milliliter bottles as “miniatures,” whereas some distillers hoped for the term “flasks” to catch on. In 1976, the then-president of DISCUS told the New York Times, “There are myriad problems in this industry, and this is one of them. We wanted to have uniform nomenclature, but it doesn’t seem to be working out that way.” His suspicion rings true today: There still isn’t a set terminology for bottle sizes beyond “handle” for 1 ¾ liters and the “fifth,” which stuck despite the volume no longer measuring to one fifth of a gallon.

After all, the switch from 757 milliliters was just a minor shrink, and the 750 milliliters are nearly identical to what were once fifths. So, whenever you hear the calling card “fifth,” know that you aren’t getting one fifth of a gallon but rather one percent less.
